narrative:
The 2017 San Francisco Giants were supposed to be a veteran contender returning to relevance, but the season unraveled almost from the first pitch. A disastrous April — the worst of the monthly records at 9-17 — set a tone that the club could never shake. Their high-priced closer Mark Melancon, signed to stabilize the bullpen, instead became the symbol of everything wrong, surrendering crushing late-inning leads in back-to-back catastrophic appearances in the season's opening days. The offense, built around an aging core, sputtered to a .689 OPS, and the pitching staff bled runs at a 4.50 ERA rate all year long.

There were fleeting moments of hope scattered through the summer. Buster Posey flashed his usual brilliance with clutch hits and timely doubles. Hunter Pence provided a pair of emotional home runs in June that briefly energized the fanbase. Eduardo Núñez, a rare bright spot in the lineup, delivered a big double in May that kept the team's slim playoff dreams alive for another day. But for every spark, the bullpen or the rotation quickly doused the flame — Melancon continued to implode, relievers like Strickland and Gearrin surrendered pivotal homers, and veterans like Jeff Samardzija and Matt Cain gave up three-run blasts at the worst possible moments.

By the trade deadline and into August, the Giants were sellers in all but official declaration. The team's 64-98 final record — the franchise's worst in decades — reflected a roster that had aged out of contention without an adequate plan for the future. The August stretch was marginally better at 13-16, but by then the season had long since lost its meaning. September brought only individual milestones and a mercifully short coda, capped by Pablo Sandoval's home run on the final day of the season — a nostalgic flourish from a former hero returning to the club, a bittersweet reminder of a championship era now firmly in the rearview mirror.

The 2017 Giants scored 137 fewer runs than they allowed, a gap that tells the whole story. A franchise that won three World Series in five years found itself at rock bottom, undone by an aging core, a broken bullpen, and a front office that bet too long on a closing window. The season's top plays were almost entirely defined by failure — blown leads, surrendered homers, and costly mistakes in high-leverage moments — a statistical portrait of a team that lost the game's most important moments with painful consistency.

chapters.title: Melancon and the Meltdown
chapters.description: The Giants' costly new closer immediately becomes the season's villain, surrendering back-to-back crushing leads in the opening days and setting a grim tone for a historically bad April.

chapters.title: Scattered Sparks in May
chapters.description: Posey and Núñez deliver clutch hits that keep hope flickering, even as the bullpen continues to undermine any momentum and the team limps to a 13-16 record.

chapters.title: Pence's Pulse and June's Chaos
chapters.description: Hunter Pence provides back-to-back emotional home runs that briefly ignite the AT&T Park crowd, but Melancon's ongoing meltdowns and a 9-18 June record ensure the playoff dream dies in the summer heat.

chapters.title: Midsummer Glimmers
chapters.description: Posey delivers a pair of clutch doubles and Conor Gillaspie chips in a home run as the team plays modestly better in July, but a brutal Albert Suárez implosion against the Dodgers encapsulates the season's futility.

chapters.title: Fading Into September
chapters.description: With the season long lost, individual moments from Posey and Hundley provide late dignity, before Sam Dyson's catastrophic blown save on the penultimate day perfectly bookends a season defined by bullpen failure — leaving Pablo Sandoval's final-day homer as a melancholy farewell.
